strongest_objection: The map's sharpest form claim, the loop Fee that holds the door → Invoice that ends the favor → Fee that holds the door, is illustrated by a case that exits the loop: the edge label says the seller 'must build a new fee' and then offers the video store whose abolished late fees 'gave way to a subscription with no door at all', and a subscription is the map's own Price that goes to sleep, not a new door fee. So the loop's only worked example is its exit, and the form inference as written is undercut by its own evidence. The loop is still a real claim (a threat priced as revenue stops being a threat, the restraint does not return, the seller needs a new door one register lower), so the repair is not to drop it but to name the exit: the loop has a fork, back to a lower door or out to a sleeping price, and stated that way the map shows more than it now claims. Two smaller failures sit under it. The seriation axis, 'how much of the work the number itself does', is false for the last four stations: a five-dollar deposit rations nothing, a small cancellation fee holds no door, and the decoy and the rack rate work precisely by being high, so the far end of the itinerary is not 'magnitude irrelevant' but 'never collected', a different principle stapled to the first. And Price that names the wrong payer bundles three mechanisms (a different payer, a hidden payee, and the same buyer billed at a later point), which its own outgoing edge exposes, since the overdrafter gets a very loud bill and does not sleep.

items.item: Price that names the wrong payer: a price at one point set to hide a payment somewhere else, so the buyer cannot see whose interest the seller serves, as the free checking account paid by overdraft fees, the free search paid by the advertiser who is the actual customer, and the prison phone call priced high so that the price pays the jailer a commission; the carrier is the bundle or the tie, and the clearing story reads each price alone when the pair is the instrument.
items.why: The three cases do not share a mechanism as written: the advertiser is a different payer, the jailer is a hidden payee, and the overdrafter is the same buyer billed at a later point. The handle fits only the first. What the three actually share is that the visible price is designed to produce a payment elsewhere, and that other payment is what the seller optimizes. Stated that way the item has one mechanism and gains the discriminator it lacked (a price merely collected later is still the price the seller designs for), and the edge to Price that goes to sleep holds for exactly the cases where the user is not the payer.
items.repair: Price that names the wrong payer: the price the buyer sees is set to produce a payment somewhere else, and that other payment, not the visible one, is what the seller designs for, so the buyer cannot see whose interest the seller serves, as the free checking account built to produce overdraft fees, the free search paid by the advertiser who is the actual customer, and the prison phone call priced high because the jailer who awarded the contract takes a commission from every minute; the carrier is the bundle or the tie, it is not a price merely collected later, since a net-thirty invoice is still the price the seller designs for, and the clearing story reads each price alone when the pair is the instrument.

items.item: Peppercorn: the existence of any price at all, however small, moves a transfer into the register that courts and tax offices can see, as the peppercorn rent makes a lease enforceable and the one-dollar sale makes a gift into a purchase with a date and a buyer; the carrier is the contract, the magnitude is irrelevant, and the clearing story has no place for a price whose entire work is done by being nonzero.
items.why: The register is overstated: a court reads whether consideration exists and not how much, but a tax office or an assessor reads how much and looks straight through a one-dollar sale to the gift beneath it (a bargain sale to a relative is taxed as a gift). So the peppercorn works on exactly the witness that reads existence and fails against any witness that reads magnitude. That is a sharper discriminator than 'the magnitude is irrelevant', and it is the same fact from the other side, so the strangeness is kept rather than tamed.
items.repair: Peppercorn: the existence of any price at all, however small, moves a transfer into the register a court can see, as the peppercorn rent makes a lease enforceable and the one-dollar sale gives a gift a buyer, a date, and a warranty to sue on; the carrier is the contract, the magnitude is irrelevant to a witness that reads only whether a price exists and useless against one that reads how much, since the tax office and the assessor look through a dollar sale to the gift beneath it, and the clearing story has no place for a price whose entire work is done by being nonzero.

items.item: Decoy that must not sell: an item priced so that its neighbor looks right, whose success is measured in zero sales, as the four-hundred-dollar bottle on the wine list exists to make the ninety-dollar bottle the sensible choice and the largest popcorn exists to sell the middle one; the carrier is the menu, and the clearing story calls an unsold item a mispricing when it is the one item doing its job. Adjacent to first-mover-forecloses' anchoring of a price expectation, which is about who sets the scale first; this is about a price that works by being declined.
items.why: 'Success is measured in zero sales' is false in both of the item's own cases: the restaurant is glad to sell the four-hundred-dollar bottle and the largest popcorn sells all day. The true strangeness, stated at the end of the item, is that the price works by being declined and needs no sale; that survives, and 'must not sell' can stay as the operator's rule (price it so it will not, and shrug if it does). The repair also adds the discriminator that separates it from Rack rate, its closest neighbor: the decoy's unpaid number belongs to a neighboring good, the rack rate's to the very good on sale.
items.repair: Decoy that must not sell: an item priced so that its neighbor looks right, whose job is done by being declined and needs no sale, as the four-hundred-dollar bottle on the wine list exists to make the ninety-dollar bottle the sensible choice and the largest popcorn exists to sell the middle one; the carrier is the menu, the unpaid number belongs to a neighboring good rather than to the good it sells, and the clearing story calls an unsold item a mispricing when it is the one item doing its job. Adjacent to first-mover-forecloses' anchoring of a price expectation, which is about who sets the scale first; this is about a price that works by being declined.

items.item: Rack rate: a list price nobody pays, kept so that every real price can be a discount from it, granted selectively and felt as a favor, and so that a third party can be billed against it, as the hotel's posted rate and the hospital chargemaster that only the uninsured and the insurer's formula ever meet; the carrier is the discount, the price is for the very good on sale yet clears nothing for anyone, and removing it does not lower prices but removes the seller's power to give.
items.why: Tested as the right-hand neighbor of Decoy that must not sell; separates on whose good the unpaid number belongs to and on the third party billed against it (see neighbor_test). 'Removing it does not lower prices but removes the seller's power to give' is the map's best operator sentence and is kept as an authored claim.

items.item: Velvet rope: a price set high enough that the crowd it admits becomes the product for everyone in it, as the nine-dollar coffee keeps the coworking floor quiet by pricing out anyone who came to sit for an afternoon, and the private bank's minimum balance sells its other clients' company; the carrier is the buyer population, the seller wants fewer buyers of a particular sort, and the quantity a clearing price would sell is the failure rather than the goal.
items.why: Kept, with one caveat for the repairer: the nine-dollar coworking coffee is the weakest case, since pricing out the afternoon sitter charges the seat-hours they consume and is close to the congestion charge the ledger rejected as clearing on a corrected cost. The private bank's minimum balance is the true rope: wealth is a proxy screen on the sort of person, the seller would forgo the money, and a rich loud client is the failure the number cannot prevent. The item's own words already say 'fewer buyers of a particular sort', so the mechanism survives; if a case is swapped, swap the coffee.

neighbor_test.left: Decoy that must not sell: an item priced so that its neighbor looks right, whose success is measured in zero sales, as the four-hundred-dollar bottle on the wine list exists to make the ninety-dollar bottle the sensible choice and the largest popcorn exists to sell the middle one; the carrier is the menu, and the clearing story calls an unsold item a mispricing when it is the one item doing its job. Adjacent to first-mover-forecloses' anchoring of a price expectation, which is about who sets the scale first; this is about a price that works by being declined.
neighbor_test.right: Rack rate: a list price nobody pays, kept so that every real price can be a discount from it, granted selectively and felt as a favor, and so that a third party can be billed against it, as the hotel's posted rate and the hospital chargemaster that only the uninsured and the insurer's formula ever meet; the carrier is the discount, the price is for the very good on sale yet clears nothing for anyone, and removing it does not lower prices but removes the seller's power to give.
neighbor_test.separating_case: Both are prices nobody pays that make the paid price look right, and the author's discriminator ('success measured in zero sales' against 'nobody pays') does not separate them, since the hotel is as glad of a walk-in at rack as the restaurant is of the four-hundred-dollar bottle. The case that separates them is the hospital MRI: chargemaster three thousand, negotiated six hundred, the insurer's statement reading 'you saved two thousand four hundred', the uninsured billed the full three thousand. There is no neighboring good on that menu; the unpaid number belongs to the very scan being sold, and its work runs through the discount felt as a favor and the third party billed against it, which no decoy can do. Run the other way, the cinema's large popcorn has no discount, no favor, and no third party; its number belongs to a different good and works only through the comparison set. So: decoy, an unpaid price on a neighbor; rack rate, an unpaid price on the thing itself. The repair to Decoy writes that line into the item.

boundary_case: The price-match guarantee ('we will beat any advertised price by ten percent') is tempting: it is a number that addresses rivals rather than buyers, tells them a cut is pointless, and can hold a whole street's prices up, which looks like a price doing something other than clearing and sits near Price for the stranger's eyes. Ruling: out. The instrument is a clause about other sellers' prices, not this price's magnitude, shape, existence, or collection; it is the identity-fence ruling seen from the other side (a rule about the number is not the number) and it belongs with first-mover-forecloses' scorched-earth signal as a move. The test sharpens the type usefully: the map admits the form of a quote (Quote that cannot be compared) but not a promise about a quote. It also exposes a member the map lacks without duplicating one: a posted price addressed to rivals as a coordination signal (the fuel price on the pole that the station across the road reads before it reads its own costs) would be Price for the stranger's eyes with the stranger a competitor, and is not the same as the guarantee.

seriation.note: The itinerary holds and both claimed adjacencies teach. Invoice that ends the favor → Peppercorn is the map's best adjacency, one nonzero number read by two registers, and the Peppercorn repair makes it teach more (the court reads existence, the tax office reads magnitude, the friends read neither). The hinge Deposit that comes back → Fee that holds the door is real: money stops changing hands on the good path. What does not hold is the axis sentence. 'How much of the work the number itself does' orders the first three segments and then fails for all four stations of the fourth: the deposit rations by its size, the door fee threatens by its size, and the decoy and the rack rate work by being high, so 'magnitude irrelevant' is true of the peppercorn alone. The far end is not 'the number does nothing' but 'the number is never collected', a second principle stapled to the first. Repair the axis, not the order: name it 'which feature of the price carries the work: its magnitude, its shape, its bare existence, or its non-collection', with the same endpoints (Velvet rope, where the magnitude is the whole instrument; Rack rate, where the number is collected from no one). No station moves.

edges.why: The label's own illustration exits the loop it closes: a subscription is Price that goes to sleep, not a new door fee. The loop is a real claim and is kept; the repair names the fork so the form inference matches the evidence, and gives the loop a case that actually loops (fines abolished, replacement cost billed after thirty days is a new door one register lower), phrased as an illustration rather than a history.
edges.repair_label: If the option is now openly priced and the old restraint does not return when the fee is dropped, a seller who wants the door shut again must build a new fee, and every new fee begins as a threat the seller hopes never to collect, one register lower each turn, as the library that abolishes fines and instead bills replacement cost after thirty days; the loop has one exit, which is to give up the door for a price that goes to sleep, as the video store's abolished late fees gave way to a subscription with no door at all.

edges.from_handle: Price that names the wrong payer
edges.why: The antecedent ('if the user is not the payer') can fail and does: the overdrafter is user and payer and is woken hard. That is not a flaw in the edge but the evidence that the source item bundled mechanisms; with the item repaired, the edge holds for the advertiser and the jailer and correctly excludes the overdrafter. Keep the label; the repairer must update its from-string to the repaired item text.

A genuine incompatibility between seriation neighbors that the sequence hides: testimony's success is demand at the high number, which is the rope's failure. Antecedent fails whenever the price does only one job.

modality_problems: Edge Invoice that ends the favor → Fee that holds the door: the video-store clause is presented as the loop's illustration but is its exit, and the actual history (late fees dropped under subscription competition, then a disputed restocking fee) is a reading; the boundary claim hedges it as 'one reading of one industry's history', and the repaired label keeps that modality by treating it as the exit.
Peppercorn: 'the register that courts and tax offices can see' promotes a half-truth; courts honor nominal consideration, tax offices look through it. Repaired in the item.
Decoy that must not sell: 'success is measured in zero sales' is asserted as the mechanism and is false in both of the item's cases. Repaired in the item.

Tier that makes the kind: 'the third-class carriage made a class of passenger out of a fare' is an illustrative reading asserted as history; the 1844 statute fixed a fare and a minimum accommodation together, so fare and carriage co-defined the class. Not a repair, since the bicycle case carries the mechanism cleanly, but the case belongs in the boundary claim's list of simplified histories.

Price that goes to sleep: 'the market never clears again after the first purchase' is an authored overstatement (renewal notices, price rises, and card expiries all wake it); acceptable as the item's register, but it is a claim, not an observation.
duplication: none. Item-level adjacencies are real and already named in the text: Price for the stranger's eyes beside exchange-ontologies' Precedent, Price that goes to sleep beside leverage-discoveries' default, Decoy beside first-mover-forecloses' anchoring, and Peppercorn and Price for the stranger's eyes are witness-shaped and lean toward witness-architectures, which the author flags in next_crossfield_opening. None restates a grown list; each says what the price itself does that the neighbor list does not.
best_unresolved_seed: The map already contains a contradiction it has not noticed, and it is the best thing in it: Mates' rates says the guest-friend's token payment 'says this is not a purchase', and Peppercorn says the one-dollar sale 'makes a gift into a purchase'. The same nominal number is read oppositely by two witnesses at once, the friends and the court, and the tax office reads it a third way. So a price is not addressed to a market but to a set of readers who disagree about what it means, and the operator's question becomes: which witness am I pricing for, and what does the number say to the ones I am not? That fork (one number, several registers, each reading a different feature: existence, magnitude, or the fact of haggling) would also resolve the ledger's bride-price residue, which is a payment that constitutes an alliance to kin, a purchase to a court, and nothing at all to a market; it connects directly to witness-architectures and is a list, not a repair to this map.
independent_review_line: Fable critic: admitted after repairing three items (the wrong-payer item's bundled mechanism, the peppercorn's overstated witness, and the decoy's false zero-sales claim), relabeling one edge whose illustration exited the loop it was meant to close, and renaming the seriation axis from how much work the number does to which feature of the price carries it.
